_meta.note: SAMPLE RULES DATA for the BGN Documentation Reference — classic public-domain board & parlor games. Rules written as a concise table reference; always defer to your physical rulebook for tournament rulings. This file demonstrates the 'groups = games' pattern for classic board games.

entries.name: Setting Up the Board
entries.subtitle: The board is placed with a light square on each player's right

blocks.t: Each player starts with **16 pieces**: 8 pawns, 2 rooks, 2 knights, 2 bishops, 1 queen, and 1 king. White's pieces line up on rank 1, Black's on rank 8, with pawns on the second/eighth ranks.

items: Back row (from left, White's side): Rook, Knight, Bishop, Queen, King, Bishop, Knight, Rook.
The **queen goes on her own color** (White queen on a light square, Black queen on a dark square).
Pawns occupy the entire rank in front of the back row.

entries.name: How the Pieces Move
entries.subtitle: Each piece has its own movement pattern

rows: 1 square forward (2 on its first move)
Any number of squares along a rank or file
An L-shape: 2 + 1 squares, jumping over pieces
Any number of squares along a diagonal
Any number of squares along rank, file, or diagonal

entries.name: Special Moves
entries.subtitle: Castling, en passant, and promotion

blocks.name: Castling
blocks.t: One move per game: the king moves 2 squares toward a rook and the rook jumps over to the square the king crossed. Only allowed if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, the king isn't in check, and the king doesn't pass through or land on an attacked square.

blocks.name: En Passant
blocks.t: If an enemy pawn moves 2 squares and lands beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had moved only 1 square — but only on the very next move.

blocks.name: Promotion
blocks.t: A pawn reaching the last rank immediately becomes a queen, rook, bishop, or knight of the same color (queen is the usual choice).

entries.name: Check, Checkmate, and Draws
entries.subtitle: How the game ends

blocks.t: A king **in check** is attacked by an enemy piece. You must respond by moving out of check, blocking the attack, or capturing the attacker. If you can't, it's **checkmate** and you lose.

items: **Stalemate** — the player to move has no legal move but isn't in check: a draw.
**Insufficient material** — king vs king, or king + minor piece vs king: a draw.
**Repetition** — the same position occurs three times: a draw.
**50-move rule** — no capture or pawn move in 50 moves by each player: a draw.

entries.name: Setup & The Bank
entries.subtitle: Get ready to become a property mogul

blocks.t: Each player chooses a token and starts with **$1,500** in cash from the Bank. The Bank holds all money not in play, the title deeds, and the houses and hotels.
The **Banker** manages the money and auctions — but can play normally too. Shuffle the Chance and Community Chest decks. Each player rolls the dice; the highest roller goes first.

entries.name: Turn Structure
entries.subtitle: Roll, move, and act

blocks.t: On your turn, roll both dice, move that many spaces, and resolve the space you land on. If you roll **doubles**, take another turn; roll doubles **three times in a row** and you go directly to Jail.

items: Landing on an **unowned property** lets you buy it (at the printed price) or the Bank auctions it to the highest bidder.
Landing on an **owned property** means paying rent to its owner.
Landing on a **tax** square pays the bank.

entries.name: Rent, Houses & Hotels
entries.subtitle: Monopoly on the block

blocks.t: Rent is paid when someone lands on your property. A property with no buildings charges its base rent; owning **all the properties in a color group** doubles the unimproved rent.

Build **houses** (up to 4) and then a **hotel** evenly — you can't place a second house on a property until every property in the color group has one. Houses cost the printed price and are returned to the Bank (at half price) when you mortgage.
**Railroads** charge $25/$50/$100/$200 for owning 1/2/3/4. **Utilities** charge 4× your dice roll if you own one, 10× if you own both.

entries.name: Chance, Community Chest & Jail
entries.subtitle: Cards, corners, and incarceration

blocks.t: Landing on a **Chance or Community Chest** square draws the top card and follows its instructions (pay, collect, move, or Go to Jail), then places it face-down at the bottom of the deck.

You land in **Jail** by rolling doubles three times, drawing a card, or landing on Go to Jail. Get out by paying **$50**, using a **Get Out of Jail Free card**, or rolling doubles on a turn. While in Jail you may still collect rent on your own properties.
**Free Parking** (house rules vary) collects nothing in the standard rules — taxes and fines go to the Bank, not the board's center.

entries.name: Bankruptcy & Winning
entries.subtitle: Last player standing

blocks.t: If you owe more than you can pay (cash + properties at mortgage value), you're **bankrupt** and out of the game. Your properties go to the player you owed (or the Bank if you owed the Bank); mortgages pass along as-is.
The game continues until **only one player remains solvent** — they win. (House rules may set a time limit and count total assets.)

entries.name: Scrabble Setup
entries.subtitle: Seven tiles each, everyone plays

blocks.t: Each player draws **7 tiles** from the bag. Play passes clockwise, and the player with the tile closest to A (blank counts best) goes first.
The first word must cover the **center star** square (which counts as a double word score). Before the first word, any player may **challenge** the play to the dictionary.

refs.license: Public domain sample — verify your edition

entries.text: scrabble setup seven tiles each everyone plays center star

entries.name: Playing Words & Scoring
entries.subtitle: Build, score, and refill

blocks.t: On your turn, form a **single word** (minimum 2 letters) horizontally or vertically, reading left-to-right or top-to-bottom. Every letter must connect to the existing words — words are formed along and across the play.

**Score** every new word formed: each tile's letter value, doubled or tripled by the premium squares its letters cover. **Double/triple letter** applies to the tile, **double/triple word** multiplies the whole word. Play all 7 tiles and you get a **50-point bingo bonus**.
After playing, draw back up to 7 tiles. You may instead **pass** or **exchange** tiles (costs your turn).

entries.name: Endgame & Challenges
entries.subtitle: Finishing the game

blocks.t: The game ends when the **bag is empty and one player uses their last tile**, or when every player passes twice in a row. A player may **challenge** an opponent's word before the turn ends; if the word isn't in the agreed dictionary it's removed and the turn is forfeited (with tiles returned).
Final scores subtract each player's **unplayed tile values** (with those values added to the player who emptied their rack), then the highest total wins.

entries.name: Risk Setup
entries.subtitle: Claim the world

blocks.t: Each player picks a color, and the dice decide who places first. Players take turns placing **one army at a time** on the board until every territory is claimed (each territory holds at least 1 army).
Players then take turns adding their **starting reinforcement bonus** — for a standard game, each player receives a set number of armies to place at the start of their first turn.

refs.license: Public domain sample — verify your edition

entries.text: risk setup claim the world army territory reinforcement

entries.name: Turn Structure
entries.subtitle: Reinforce, attack, fortify

blocks.t: Each turn has three phases: **Reinforcement** — add armies based on your territories (1 per territory ÷ 3, min 3) plus continent bonuses and risk card sets. **Attack** — attack adjacent enemy territories. **Fortify** — move armies between adjacent territories you control (once per turn).
Continent bonuses: North America +5, South America +2, Europe +5, Africa +3, Asia +7, Australia +2.

entries.name: Attacking
entries.subtitle: Dice determine the battle

blocks.t: Attack with **up to 3 dice** from a territory holding more than 1 army. The defender rolls **up to 2 dice**. Compare highest-to-highest (then next-to-next): the attacker loses an army on ties, otherwise the defender loses one army per comparison.
If the defender's last army is eliminated you **may move your attacking armies** into the conquered territory (at least 1 must stay behind).

entries.name: Cards & Winning
entries.subtitle: Trading in sets

blocks.t: When you conquer at least one territory on your turn, you take a **Risk card** (a territory card plus a bonus type). Trade sets of 3 cards — any 3 of a kind, or one of each type — for extra armies at the start of a turn (4, 8, 12, …; the 5th set is 15).
**Winning:** capture every territory on the board and eliminate all opponents. That's the only way — total world domination.

entries.name: Cluedo Setup
entries.subtitle: Whodunit?

blocks.t: One **murder** is set up in secret: shuffle the suspects (6), weapons (6), and rooms (9) decks separately, and without looking place one card of each type into the confidential envelope. The remaining cards are dealt to players (equally, extras face-down in front of the board).
Each player chooses a token and a starting location (different rooms). Players keep their hands hidden — the goal is to deduce the three cards in the envelope.

entries.text: cluedo setup whodunit suspects weapons rooms confidential envelope

entries.name: Turns, Suggestions & Accusations
entries.subtitle: Move, suggest, and accuse

blocks.t: On your turn roll the die, move that many squares (through rooms and corridors), then in a room you may make a **suggestion**: name a suspect, weapon, and the room you're in. The next player who holds any of those cards must **secretly show one** to you.

Once you're confident, on your turn you may make an **accusation** naming any suspect/weapon/room (not necessarily your location). Check the envelope in secret: if correct, reveal it and win. If wrong, you're out of the game (but may still answer suggestions).

entries.name: Backgammon Setup
entries.subtitle: Two armies race around the board

blocks.t: Each player has **15 checkers** on a 24-point board, arranged in the classic opening position: 2 on the 24-point, 5 on the 13-point, 3 on the 8-point, and 5 on the 6-point (opposing players mirror). Points are numbered 1–24 in each player's direction of travel.
Your checkers move **counter-clockwise** from your 24-point to your 1-point (the home board), then off the board by bearing off.

refs.license: Public domain sample — verify your edition

entries.text: backgammon setup two armies race around the board 15 checkers 24 point

entries.name: Movement, Hits & Entering
entries.subtitle: The dice drive everything

blocks.t: Roll **two dice** and move a checker that many points (each die is a separate move — you can split the moves across two checkers). **Doubles** let you move four times that value.

A point with **two or more** enemy checkers is blocked. Landing on a **single enemy checker** hits it: it moves to the **bar** and must re-enter on your 24-point side on your next roll before any other move.
Once all your checkers are in your home board you **bear off**: dice that match or exceed a checker's point value remove it. The first to bear off all 15 wins.

refs.license: Public domain sample — verify your edition

entries.text: movement hits and entering backgammon the dice drive everything doubles bar bear off

entries.name: The Doubling Cube
entries.subtitle: Raising the stakes

blocks.t: The **doubling cube** shows 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Before rolling, a player may offer the opponent double-or-nothing. The opponent may **take** (the game is now worth double, and only the taker may double next) or **drop** (concede the game at the current stake).
A **gammon** (the loser hasn't borne off any checkers) doubles the stake; a **backgammon** (loser has a checker on the bar or in the opponent's board) triples it.
